title: The problem: the deaths and the near-deaths
plain_summary: For every mother who dies in childbirth, several more nearly die. Counting both - deaths and these 'near-misses' - shows where care is breaking down. Tanzania's maternal death rate had been rising, from about 454 to 556 per 100,000 births.

title: What the study did
plain_summary: At one busy hospital - Dodoma Regional Referral - researchers reviewed four months of records (October 2015 to January 2016). Of 3,600 women admitted for pregnancy reasons, 140 had a severe maternal outcome by WHO criteria: either they died or they nearly did.

title: How many, and how close
plain_summary: Of the 140 women with a severe outcome, 16 died and 124 survived a life-threatening complication. That's about 8 near-misses for every death, and roughly 1 in 9 of these critically ill women didn't make it.

title: What nearly killed them
plain_summary: Three quarters of the severe cases came from direct obstetric causes. Postpartum bleeding and high-blood-pressure disorders led. Among the women who died, hypertensive disorders, bleeding, severe anaemia and heart problems each took a heavy share.

title: The babies
plain_summary: When the mother is in crisis, the baby often is too. Among these pregnancies there were 39 perinatal deaths, and about 45% ended in a poor outcome for the newborn - stillbirth, early death, or complications at birth.

title: What helped, and what to fix
plain_summary: Women who got prompt, protocol-based care from a skilled team were far less likely to die. But over half needed a blood transfusion and about 40% of them got too little blood. Stronger emergency obstetric care and reliable blood supply are the clear levers.
